title: IBD and Autoimmune Overlap: What Patients Should Know
description: How Crohn's and ulcerative colitis relate to other immune-mediated conditions, what overlap means, and questions for your care team. Education only.
alts: Calm setting for learning about IBD and immune overlap
share: IBD and autoimmune overlap: patient education, not a diagnosis tool.
body:
People searching IBD autoimmune, Crohn's autoimmune disease, or ulcerative colitis immune system often want one clear answer: is IBD an autoimmune disease, and why do other immune conditions show up nearby? Clinicians usually describe IBD as an immune-mediated inflammatory disease. The immune system drives gut inflammation, and related problems can appear outside the intestine.

What "overlap" means in plain language

Overlap does not mean every person with Crohn's or colitis will develop another autoimmune diagnosis. It means shared immune pathways, genetics, and inflammation can raise the chance of joint, skin, eye, liver, or other issues. Some problems track with gut flares. Others need their own specialist plan.

  • Extraintestinal manifestations: immune activity outside the gut linked to IBD
  • Co-occurring conditions: separate diagnoses that appear more often with IBD
  • Medication effects: steroids, biologics, and immunosuppressants that change infection and vaccine planning

Where to start reading

Map common sites with extraintestinal manifestations. For joints, see joint pain and arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis and IBD. For eyes and skin, see uveitis and EN and PG skin flares.

Questions for your team

  • Which of my symptoms look gut-driven vs a separate immune problem?
  • Do I need rheumatology, dermatology, ophthalmology, or hepatology?
  • Could my IBD therapy also help an overlap condition?

Related: autoimmune associations hub, research sources, visit prep.

title: PSC and IBD: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis Explained
description: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's: why liver tests matter, monitoring themes, and clinic questions. Education only.
alts: Quiet rest representing fatigue and liver monitoring in IBD
share: PSC and IBD: patient-level overview of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
body:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic disease of the bile ducts. It is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. Not everyone with IBD develops PSC, and not everyone with PSC has classic IBD symptoms at first. Education helps you ask better questions; only your clinicians diagnose and monitor the condition.

Why IBD teams watch the liver

PSC can raise liver enzymes, cause itching, fatigue, or infections in the bile ducts, and needs long-term imaging and lab follow-up. Colon cancer surveillance schedules may differ when PSC and colitis travel together. Bring abnormal liver tests to attention even if stools feel quiet.

  • Ask what your ALT, AST, ALP, and bilirubin trends mean
  • Report new itching, yellowing eyes, fever with right-upper pain, or dark urine
  • Confirm who leads monitoring: GI, hepatology, or both

How this fits other immune topics

PSC is one piece of the broader IBD autoimmune overlap picture. Fatigue can have many causes; see fatigue and autoimmune IBD and fatigue and brain fog.

Questions to bring

  • Do my labs suggest bile-duct disease that needs imaging?
  • How often should we check liver tests and colonoscopy if PSC is confirmed?
  • Which symptoms should trigger same-day or urgent calls?

Related: autoimmune hepatitis and IBD, trusted research sources, visit prep.

title: Ankylosing Spondylitis and IBD: Axial Joint Pain Explained
description: Ankylosing spondylitis and spondyloarthritis with Crohn's or colitis: morning stiffness, back pain, and rheumatology coordination. Education only.
alts: Movement and joint care themes for IBD-related back pain
share: Ankylosing spondylitis and IBD: axial pain education for patients.
body:
Lower-back pain and morning stiffness push many IBD patients to search ankylosing spondylitis IBD or Crohn's spine pain. Axial spondyloarthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis (AS), can overlap with Crohn's and ulcerative colitis. Peripheral joint pain is common too; this article focuses on the spine and sacroiliac pattern.

Patterns worth reporting

  • Deep buttock or low-back pain that eases with movement and worsens with rest
  • Morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes
  • Night pain that wakes you for reasons other than bathroom trips
  • Heel, chest-wall, or Achilles tendon pain alongside IBD

Not every backache is inflammatory. Mechanical strain, deconditioning, and steroid-related bone changes still matter. Start with IBD joint pain and arthritis and leg and knee pain.

Care team coordination

Rheumatology often co-manages axial disease. Some biologics used for IBD also treat spondyloarthritis; your teams decide together. NSAIDs that help AS may irritate the gut, so do not self-start high-dose ibuprofen without guidance.

Questions for clinic

  • Do I need imaging or HLA-B27 discussion, or is this mechanical pain?
  • Which pain medicines are safer with my IBD history?
  • Could one therapy cover gut and spine inflammation?

Related: EIM map, psoriasis and IBD, visit prep.

title: Psoriasis and IBD: Shared Inflammation, Shared Questions
description: Why psoriasis and psoriatic patterns appear with Crohn's or colitis, skin flares vs medication rashes, and dermatology tips. Education only.
alts: Soft lighting for skin and inflammation education in IBD
share: Psoriasis and IBD connection: patient education overview.
body:
Searches for psoriasis and Crohn's or ulcerative colitis skin rash climb because skin and gut inflammation can travel in the same immune neighborhood. Psoriasis is not the same as erythema nodosum or pyoderma gangrenosum, but all deserve a clear description for your clinicians.

What patients often notice

  • Thick, scaly plaques on elbows, knees, scalp, or lower back
  • Nail pitting or joint stiffness with skin changes
  • New rashes after starting or switching IBD medicines

Medication reactions and infection-related rashes can look similar. Do not stop a biologic because of a rash without clinician advice. For nodular shin lesions or ulcerating skin, read EN and PG.

Why the connection matters

Shared inflammatory pathways mean dermatology and gastroenterology sometimes choose therapies that address both skin and gut disease. Joint involvement can point toward axial disease or peripheral arthritis. See the wider frame in autoimmune overlap.

Questions to ask

  • Is this psoriasis, an IBD skin manifestation, or a drug effect?
  • Should dermatology join my care team now?
  • Which therapies help both skin and IBD for my case?

Related: extraintestinal manifestations, research sources.

title: Celiac Screening with IBD: Before You Go Gluten-Free
description: Celiac disease overlap with Crohn's or colitis: why screen before long gluten-free trials, dietitian coordination, and clinic questions.
alts: Fresh foods representing gluten and nutrition decisions in IBD
share: Celiac screening with IBD: test before long gluten-free trials.
body:
Gluten-free eating is common advice on social media. For people with IBD, the smarter first step is often celiac screening. Celiac disease is more common in people with IBD than in the general population, and going gluten-free for months can make antibody testing harder to interpret.

Screen first, then decide

Ask your GI team about celiac blood tests while you are still eating gluten. Some people also need duodenal biopsies. If celiac is confirmed, a strict gluten-free diet is medical therapy, not a trend. If celiac is ruled out, wheat or FODMAP sensitivity may still matter for you personally.

Build on gluten, wheat, and IBD and our guide on when to stop an elimination diet.

Diet coordination tips

  • Work with an IBD-experienced dietitian before cutting entire food groups for months
  • Watch fiber, iron, and B vitamins if packaged gluten-free foods dominate your plate
  • Log symptoms in IBDPal or a notebook so reintroduction has data

Questions for clinic

  • Have we screened for celiac with me still eating gluten?
  • If tests are negative, what time-limited trial makes sense?
  • How do we protect nutrition if I need a gluten-free plan?

Related: nutrition hub, anti-inflammatory diet guide, micronutrient deficiencies.

title: Extraintestinal Manifestations of IBD: A Patient Map
description: Extraintestinal manifestations in Crohn's and colitis: joints, eyes, skin, liver, mouth, and bones with links to deeper IBDPal guides.
alts: Overview visual for IBD symptoms beyond the gut
share: Extraintestinal manifestations of IBD: a patient-friendly map.
body:
Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) are IBD-related problems outside the intestine. They do not replace a gastroenterologist's judgment, but naming the map helps you report symptoms earlier.

Common sites

  • Joints: peripheral arthritis, axial / AS patterns, leg and knee pain
  • Eyes: uveitis and eye inflammation
  • Skin: erythema nodosum and pyoderma, psoriasis overlap
  • Liver and bile ducts: PSC, autoimmune hepatitis themes
  • Mouth: canker sores and oral IBD
  • Bones and clots: bone health, clot risk awareness

What to do with this map

Track which symptoms rise with gut flares and which stay independent. Bring dates, photos of skin lesions (if appropriate), and a medicine list to clinic. Use autoimmune associations for the wider reading list.

Seek urgent care guidance for

  • Sudden vision change or painful light-sensitive eye
  • Rapidly expanding painful skin ulcer
  • Chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or one-sided leg swelling
  • Yellowing skin with fever or severe abdominal pain

Related: red flags hub, autoimmune overlap.

title: Autoimmune Hepatitis Themes in People with IBD
description: Autoimmune hepatitis concepts for Crohn's and colitis readers: why liver labs matter and when hepatology joins the team. Short education.
alts: Restful scene for liver health education in IBD
share: Autoimmune hepatitis themes with IBD: education only.
body:
Liver enzyme changes in IBD have many causes: medicines, fatty liver, viral infection, bile-duct disease such as PSC, or less often autoimmune hepatitis patterns. This short article is for orientation, not self-diagnosis.

Why the distinction matters

Autoimmune hepatitis is treated differently from PSC and from drug-induced liver injury. Your team may order autoantibody panels, imaging, or a biopsy. Immunosuppression plans can overlap with IBD therapy, so GI and hepatology need a shared timeline.

  • Report fatigue, itching, jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools
  • Keep a list of new supplements and over-the-counter products
  • Ask which liver tests to repeat and how soon

Overlap reading

Place this beside autoimmune overlap and fatigue in autoimmune IBD. Medication side effects still belong in the differential every time labs rise.

title: Osteoporosis and Bone Health in IBD
description: Bone loss risk in Crohn's and colitis: steroids, inflammation, vitamin D, calcium, and screening questions. Patient education only.
alts: Nutrient-rich foods supporting bone health conversations in IBD
share: Osteoporosis and bone health in IBD: steroids, vitamin D, screening.
body:
People with IBD face higher rates of low bone density. Inflammation, corticosteroid courses, low vitamin D, reduced activity, and malnutrition all play roles. Searches for osteoporosis Crohn's and steroids bone loss IBD are practical, not vanity questions.

Risk themes to discuss

  • Repeated or prolonged systemic steroids
  • Active disease with weight loss or nutrient gaps
  • Low vitamin D or calcium intake
  • Postmenopausal status, smoking, or family fracture history

Pair this with vitamin D and bone nutrition and steroid taper expectations.

What teams often consider

DEXA screening timing, vitamin D repletion, weight-bearing activity when safe, and steroid-sparing IBD plans. Do not start high-dose supplements without knowing your labs and kidney history.

Questions for clinic

  • Do I meet criteria for a bone density scan?
  • What vitamin D level are we targeting?
  • How do we protect bones if I need another steroid course?

Related: micronutrient deficiencies, nutrition hub.

title: Clot Risk and Thrombosis Awareness in IBD
description: Why Crohn's and colitis raise venous clot risk during flares and hospitalization, warning signs, and questions for your team. Education only.
alts: Calm recovery setting for IBD flare and clot-risk awareness
share: IBD clot risk awareness: when to seek urgent evaluation.
body:
Active IBD inflammation raises the risk of blood clots in veins (venous thromboembolism). Hospitals often use prevention protocols during admissions. At home, knowing warning signs still matters, especially during flares, dehydration, long travel, or after surgery.

Warning signs that need urgent evaluation

  • One-sided leg swelling, warmth, or pain
  • Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain
  • Coughing blood or fainting with breathing trouble

These are emergency patterns, not wait-and-see symptoms. See also red flags and urgent care and GI vs ER.

Risk context

Flare activity, hospitalization, central lines, smoking, hormones, and prior clots can stack risk. Prevention decisions belong with your clinicians. Do not start or stop blood thinners on your own.

Related: EIM map, flare help, research sources.

title: Mouth Sores and Canker Sores in IBD
description: Oral aphthous ulcers with Crohn's or colitis: flare links, nutrition angles, and when to call dentistry or GI. Short education.
alts: Soft lighting for comfort during IBD mouth sore recovery
share: Mouth sores and canker sores in IBD: patient education.
body:
Painful mouth ulcers are a frequent extraintestinal complaint in Crohn's disease and sometimes in ulcerative colitis. They can track with gut activity, nutrient gaps, or local irritation. Viral sores and medication effects also belong on the list.

Practical steps while you wait for advice

  • Choose soft, cool foods and avoid sharp chips or acidic juices if they sting
  • Keep hydration steady; dehydration worsens mouth comfort
  • Note whether sores rise with stool flares or appear independently

Iron, B12, and folate gaps can contribute; see anemia and iron and iron nutrition guide.

Call sooner if

  • You cannot drink enough fluids because of pain
  • Ulcers last beyond two weeks or keep expanding
  • Fever, severe throat pain, or eye inflammation appears with oral sores

Related: EIM map, eye inflammation, visit prep.

title: Fatigue Across Autoimmune and IBD Life
description: Why fatigue is common in Crohn's, colitis, and overlapping immune conditions, what to track, and clinic questions beyond "just rest."
alts: Restful bedroom light for IBD and autoimmune fatigue recovery
share: Fatigue in autoimmune and IBD life: what to track for clinic.
body:
Fatigue is one of the most searched IBD symptoms, and it intensifies when arthritis, psoriasis, liver disease, or anemia join the picture. "Sleep more" is incomplete advice. Inflammation, iron deficiency, sleep disruption from urgency, depression, and medicine effects can stack.

Build a short fatigue log

  • Energy score morning and evening for two weeks
  • Night bathroom trips and sleep hours
  • New joint, skin, or eye symptoms
  • Recent steroid tapers or biologic changes

Start with fatigue and brain fog, then check anemia, bone health, and autoimmune overlap.

Questions that move care forward

  • Which labs should we recheck for anemia, thyroid, vitamin D, or inflammation?
  • Is my fatigue tracking gut activity or a separate immune problem?
  • Would rheumatology, sleep medicine, or mental health support help?

Related: associations hub, vitamin D guide.

title: Vaccines with Autoimmune Disease and Immunosuppression
description: Vaccine planning when IBD or overlapping immune disease requires biologics or immunosuppressants: timing, live vaccines, and clinic questions.
alts: Medication planning context for vaccines on immunosuppression
share: Vaccines with autoimmune disease and immunosuppression: ask your team.
body:
People managing Crohn's, colitis, or overlapping immune conditions often take medicines that change vaccine timing. Live vaccines may be restricted. Inactivated vaccines are commonly encouraged, but schedules should come from your clinicians, not a generic social post.

Core themes to review

  • Update vaccines before starting some immunosuppressants when possible
  • Ask which shots are inactivated vs live for your plan
  • Coordinate flu, COVID, pneumonia, hepatitis, and shingles decisions with GI and primary care
  • Household members may need vaccines to protect you

Deepen the IBD-specific angle in vaccines with biologics and immunosuppressants. For new therapy starts, see first 12 weeks on a biologic.

Questions before infusion or dose changes

  • Which vaccines should I complete this season?
  • Do we delay any live vaccines while I am on current therapy?
  • Who documents my vaccine record across GI and primary care?

Related: autoimmune overlap, visit prep, research sources.
